title: The same verb eases both roads
translation: [The one who gives and fears God] and affirms the best: We will ease him toward ease. But whoever is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, and denies the best: We will ease him toward hardship.
body: In **al-Bukhari**, Ali recalls Muhammad, asked about each person’s written place, saying “Carry on” and reciting these verses. **Ibn Kathir**: God rewards good intent and abandons evil intent, all by decree. Yet the wording puts easing after the deed. For **Luther**, God hardens Pharaoh through a word his corrupt will hates (Denlinger).
question: The same verb covers both roads: even the way to hardship is “eased”. What might that say about how giving or withholding grows?
source_label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4945 · Ibn Kathir on Q 92 · Denlinger on Luther
reading: W. Montgomery Watt, Free Will and Predestination in Early Islam (1948)
